issuer: New Jersey Public Employment Relations Commission (PERC)
title: P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46
text:
P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46
STATE OF NEW JERSEY
BEFORE THE PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS COMMISSION
In the Matter of
MOUNT LAUREL BOARD OF EDUCATION,
Petitioner,
-and- Docket No. SN-2026-026
MOUNT LAUREL EDUCATION ASSOCIATION,
Respondent.
SYNOPSIS
The Public Employment Relations Commission denies the
Board’s request for a restraint of binding arbitration of the
Association’s grievance challenging the Board’s denial of sick
leave and loss of pay for employees who did not submit doctor’s
notes when they sought to use sick leave for absences on the day
after the Super Bowl and/or on the day of the Super Bowl Parade.
The Commission finds that sick leave verification policies
requiring the submission of a doctor’s note are non-negotiable.
However, the Commission holds that the application of such
policies, including sick leave denial and the imposition of
penalties such as loss of pay, are legally arbitrable.
This synopsis is not part of the Commission decision. It
has been prepared for the convenience of the reader. It has been
neither reviewed nor approved by the Commission.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46
STATE OF NEW JERSEY
BEFORE THE PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS COMMISSION
In the Matter of
MOUNT LAUREL BOARD OF EDUCATION,
Petitioner,
-and- Docket No. SN-2026-026
MOUNT LAUREL EDUCATION ASSOCIATION,
Respondent.
Appearances:
For the Petitioner, Capehart Scatchard, P.A., attorneys
(Sanmathi Dev, of counsel)
For the Respondent, Selikoff & Cohen, P.A., attorneys
(Steven R. Cohen, of counsel; Hop T. Wechsler, of
counsel)
DECISION
On March 31, 2026, the Mount Laurel Board of Education
(Board) filed a scope of negotiations petition seeking a
restraint of binding arbitration of a grievance filed by the
Mount Laurel Education Association (Association). The grievance
challenges the Board’s denial of sick leave and deduction of a
day’s pay for three staff members who did not provide a doctor’s
note when they sought to use sick leave for their absences on
February 10, 2025 and/or February 14, 2025.
The Board filed a brief with exhibits and the certification
of its counsel attesting to the truth and accuracy of the

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 2.
exhibits, as well as a reply brief. The Association filed a
brief and a sur-reply brief.1/ These facts appear.
The Association represents the Board’s certified teachers,
secretaries, custodians, assistants, library aides, nurse aides,
office aides, preschool handicap aides, aides to classrooms,
aides to classrooms, applied behavior analysis trainers, signing
interpreter, technology support specialist, occupational
therapist, intervener for deaf and blind, and other titles listed
in the recognition clause of the parties’ collective negotiations
agreement (CNA). The Board and Association are parties to a CNA
with a term of July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2027.
Article 7 of the CNA sets forth the parties’ grievance
procedure. Article 7.A.1. defines a grievance as “a claim by an
employee or the Association based upon the interpretation,
application, or violation of this agreement, policies or
administrative decisions affecting terms and conditions of
employment.” The grievance procedure ends in binding
arbitration. Article 4 of the CNA is entitled “Employee Rights.”
Article 4.E. is entitled “Just Cause Provision” and provides that
no teacher or educational support personnel shall be disciplined
without just cause and that any discipline “shall be subject to
the grievance procedure.”
1/ N.J.A.C. 19:13-3.6(f) requires that all pertinent facts be
supported by certifications based upon personal knowledge.
Neither party submitted such a certification.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 3.
The Board’s Sick and Personal Leave Policy 4150/4250
provides that it “reserves the right to specify the conditions
under which leaves and absences may be taken when not otherwise
covered by the terms of a negotiated agreement.” The Policy
provides, in pertinent part:
The board reserves the right to require
sufficient proof of any professional staff
member claiming sick leave pay, including a
physician’s certification, of the
professional staff member’s illness or
disability.
Any professional staff member absent on sick
leave may be required to submit a physician’s
written statement certifying his or her
disability. Such statements may not be
presumed to establish the professional staff
member’s disability conclusively.
On February 7, 2025, in anticipation of the Philadelphia
Eagles potentially winning the Super Bowl on February 9, the
Board’s Superintendent issued a memorandum to staff entitled
“Super Bowl and Parade Absenteeism Protocols.” The memorandum
notified staff that it was “implementing protocols for the use of
sick leave for the day after the Super Bowl (Monday, February 10,
2025), as well as for the potential celebratory parade day (TBD),
should the Eagles claim victory.” The memorandum provided:
In order to address absenteeism on these
dates, we will require a doctor’s note for
anyone who calls out sick for their own
personal illness or injury. If a doctor’s
note is not provided for the aforementioned
dates your sick leave will not be approved
and subsequently will result in a dockage of
pay. Personal leave requests are being

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 4.
addressed according to district policy and
collective bargaining agreements.
On May 30, 2025, the Board’s Director of Human Resources
sent separate letters to three Association unit employees
reiterating the February 7 memorandum concerning absences the day
after the Super Bowl, and stating:
Our records show that you were absent on
Monday, February 10, 2025 to which you used a
sick day and did not provide a medical note.
I reached out to you on February 11, 2025 and
again on February 18, 2025 to request this
medical note to which you have been unable to
provide. Subsequently, your June 15, 2025
payroll will result in a day without pay of
your per diem amount of [applicable $
amount]. If this was an oversight on your
part and you indeed can provide a medical
note for your absence, please promptly
forward that medical note to my attention
before Monday, June 2, 2025 to avoid this
payroll dockage.
On June 16, 2025, the Association filed a grievance
contesting the payroll deductions for the three unit employees
for their sick day following the Eagles’ Super Bowl victory.2/
The grievance asserts that the CNA provides that while employees
may be asked to provide a sick note, it is silent on any pay
deduction due to no documentation for that sick day. The
2/ While the Board’s May 30, 2025 letters indicate February 10
(the day after the Super Bowl) as the absences for these
employees, the Association’s grievance references February
14 absences (the day of the Super Bowl Parade), and the
Board’s response to the grievance clarifies that for one
staff member the absence without a doctor’s note was
February 10 and for the other two it was February 14.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 5.
Association further argues there is no past practice of
withholding pay for an employee sick day without documentation.
On June 27, the Superintendent denied the grievance, noting that
when an employee’s absence has not been approved, “the District
has designated such a day as an unpaid day.” On July 2, the
Association advanced the grievance to the Board, asserting that
“[t]here is not a district policy or an agreement with the MLEA
that allows the district to dock a member’s pay because they
cannot provide a doctor’s note for a one day absence, due to
illness.” On July 9, the Board, through its counsel, denied the
grievance. On August 7, the Association filed a request for
binding arbitration. This petition ensued.
The Commission’s inquiry on a scope of negotiations
petition is quite narrow. We are addressing a single issue in
the abstract: whether the subject matter in dispute is within the
scope of collective negotiations. The merits of the
Association’s claimed violation of the agreement, as well as the
Board’s contractual defenses, are not in issue, because those are
matters for the arbitrator to decide if the Commission determines
that the question is one that may be arbitrated. Ridgefield Park
Ed. Ass’n v. Ridgefield Park Bd. of Ed., 78 N.J. 144, 154 (1978).
Local 195, IFPTE v. State, 88 N.J. 393 (1982), articulates
the standards for determining whether a subject is mandatorily
negotiable:

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 6.
[A] subject is negotiable between public
employers and employees when (1) the item
intimately and directly affects the work and
welfare of public employees; (2) the subject
has not been fully or partially preempted by
statute or regulation; and (3) a negotiated
agreement would not significantly interfere
with the determination of governmental
policy. To decide whether a negotiated
agreement would significantly interfere with
the determination of governmental policy, it
is necessary to balance the interests of the
public employees and the public employer.
When the dominant concern is the government’s
managerial prerogative to determine policy, a
subject may not be included in collective
negotiations even though it may intimately
affect employees’ working conditions.
[Id. at 404-405].
We must balance the parties’ interests in light of the particular
facts and arguments presented. City of Jersey City v. Jersey
City POBA, 154 N.J. 555, 574-575 (1998).
The Board asserts it has a managerial prerogative to verify
sick leave with a physician’s note and that N.J.S.A. 18A:30-4
also provides it with the right to maintain and enforce a sick
leave verification requirement. The Board argues that it has a
non-negotiable and non-arbitrable managerial prerogative to deny
paid sick leave when an employee fails to comply with the sick
leave verification procedure by not providing a doctor’s note.
The Board contends that the Association’s grievance “seeks to
avoid the natural consequences of violating the sick leave
policy.” The Board asserts that allowing negotiation over its

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 7.
sick leave verification policy would significantly interfere with
its governmental policy interest in reducing staff absenteeism.
The Association asserts that while the employer’s
establishment of a sick leave verification policy is a managerial
prerogative, the employer’s application of that policy -
including whether an employee was properly denied sick leave - is
legally arbitrable. It argues that the Board incorrectly
characterizes the grievance as a challenge to the Board’s sick
leave verification policy rather than a challenge to the Board’s
denial of sick leave and docking of a day’s pay for three
employees who were sick but did not see a doctor. The
Association contends that this case is nearly identical to a
previous Commission case involving the denial of sick leave to an
employee who did not provide a doctor’s note for the day of the
Super Bowl Parade in 2018 following the Eagles’ previous Super
Bowl victory. It asserts that the Commission must similarly find
here that the Association can arbitrate the application of the
sick leave verification policy, i.e., the denial of sick leave.
N.J.S.A. 18A:30-4 establishes a board’s ability to require a
physician’s certificate to verify sick leave. Moreover, it is
well-settled that a public employer has a managerial prerogative
to use reasonable means to verify employee illness, including
requiring the production of a doctor’s note. See e.g., Carteret
Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 2009-71, 35 NJPER 213 (¶76 2009); N.J.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 8.
State Judiciary (Ocean Vicinage), P.E.R.C. No. 2005-24, 30 NJPER
436 (¶143 2004); North Hudson Reg. Fire and Rescue, P.E.R.C. No.
2000-78, 26 NJPER 184 (¶31075 2000); City of Elizabeth, P.E.R.C.
No. 2000-42, 26 NJPER 22 (¶31007 1999); and Piscataway Tp. Bd. of
Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 82-64, 8 NJPER 95 (¶13039 1982).
However, the application of a sick leave verification
policy, e.g., whether an employee was improperly denied sick
leave, the imposition of economic sanctions such as denial of
pay, and whether just cause existed for the imposition of
disciplinary penalties for violating sick leave or absenteeism
policies, may be challenged through contractual grievance
procedures including binding arbitration. City of Burlington Bd.
of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 2019-27, 45 NJPER 242 (¶64 2019), aff’d,
2019 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 2422, 46 NJPER 226 (¶52 App. Div.
2019), certif. den., 241 N.J. 82 (2020); Monroe Tp. Bd. of Ed.,
P.E.R.C. No. 2020-51, 46 NJPER 518 (¶115 2020) (grievance
alleging “arbitrary docking of some employees’ pay” for
attendance policy violation is arbitrable); N. Hudson Reg.,
P.E.R.C. No. 2000-78, supra (“the penalties for violating sick
leave and absenteeism policies, are mandatorily negotiable”);
Elizabeth, P.E.R.C. No. 2000-42, supra (“arbitration may be
invoked” for disciplinary sanctions for absenteeism including
“docking of pay”); State of New Jersey (Treasury), P.E.R.C. No.
95-67, 21 NJPER 129 (¶26080 1995) (“what the disciplinary

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 9.
penalties will be for abusing sick leave” is mandatorily
negotiable); and Piscataway, P.E.R.C. No. 82-64, supra (“The
application of the [sick leave verification] policy, however, may
be subject to contractual grievance procedures.”)
In Teaneck Tp., P.E.R.C. No. 93-44, 19 NJPER 18 (¶24009
1992), the Commission confirmed that an employer does not need to
negotiate over “a policy of denying sick leave benefits to
employees who fail to comply with a verification requirement.”
19 NJPER at 19-20, n. 3. However, the Commission clarified that
the imposition of that policy could still be contested in
arbitration, not just based on claims of compliance with the sick
leave verification policy, but also based on claims for why there
could not be compliance. The Commission stated:
In addition, a union may arbitrate claims
that particular denials of benefits violated
the contract because an employee justifiably
could not comply with the verification
requirement or because the employee complied
and benefits were nevertheless denied. We
therefore decline to restrain arbitration to
the extent, if any, the grievance raises
these issues.
[Teaneck, 19 NJPER at 19.]
In Burlington City Bd. of Ed., P.E.R.C. No. 2019-27, supra,
the school board e-mailed staff notifying them that if they do
not come to work on February 8, 2018 (the day of the Eagles’
Super Bowl Parade) due to personal illness, then they “will be
required to provide a doctor’s note that indicates that you were

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 10.
unable to come to work due to illness.” An employee was absent
on the day of the Super Bowl Parade due to personal illness.
After the board requested a doctor’s note to verify his illness,
he responded that he did not see a doctor because he had the flu
and they do not want people with the flu in their offices. The
board denied his sick leave for February 8 and advised him it
would be either an unpaid leave absence or a personal business
absence. The union filed a grievance challenging the denial of
sick leave for that employee and all similarly situated
employees. The board filed a petition seeking to restrain
binding arbitration. The Commission, although finding that the
board has a statutory and managerial right to require a doctor’s
note to verify sick leave, denied the board’s request to restrain
arbitration. Citing Commission precedent holding that “the
application of a sick leave verification policy . . . may be
challenged through contractual grievance procedures,” we found
that the grievance challenged the denial of the employee’s sick
leave after he failed to obtain a doctor’s note, not the board’s
right to establish the sick leave verification policy.
On appeal, the Appellate Division affirmed the Commission’s
decision and the arbitrability of challenges to the application
of sick leave verification policies. The Court held:
Whether an employer may impose a disciplinary
penalty in applying a sick leave verification
policy may be reviewed through binding
arbitration. New Jersey State Judiciary

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 11.
(Ocean Vicinage), P.E.R.C. No. 2005-24, 30
NJPER ¶143, 2004 N.J. PERC LEXIS 168 at 9-10
(2004). The Board argued PERC erred in
allowing arbitration of its non-negotiable
right to establish a sick leave verification
policy. However, that is not the subject of
the Association’s grievance. The Association
challenged the application of the sick leave
verification policy to Association members
absent on February 8, 2018. . . . PERC’s
decision that the Association’s grievance is
arbitrable is fully supported by the evidence
in the record.
[Burlington City Bd. of Ed., 2019 N.J. Super.
Unpub. LEXIS 2422, *7-8.]
Here, as in Burlington City Bd. of Ed., the Association has
clarified that its grievance does not challenge the Board’s
managerial prerogative to request doctor’s notes to verify sick
leave absences on the day of the Eagles Super Bowl Parade.3/
Rather, similar to Burlington, the Association’s grievance
challenges the application of the Board’s sick leave verification
policy, specifically the deduction of a day’s pay from the
paychecks of three employees who did not provide a doctor’s note
for the days they sought to use sick leave during the week after
the Eagles’ 2025 Super Bowl victory. Accordingly, consistent
with Burlington and the above-cited Commission precedent, the
Association’s grievance is legally arbitrable. See, e.g., Monroe
Tp. Bd. of Ed.; N. Hudson Reg.; Elizabeth; State of New Jersey
(Treasury); Piscataway, and Teaneck.
3/ Or, in this case, additionally for the day after the Super
Bowl for one employee.

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 12.
Finally, we find the Board’s reliance on City of Newark,
P.E.R.C. No. 85-26, 10 NJPER 551 (¶15256 1984), to be misplaced.
In that case, certain employees did not sign new forms the board
was requiring employees to complete to certify to the reasons for
their requested sick or funeral leave. The case did not involve
the application of a policy requiring the submission of a
doctor’s note, and sick and funeral leave benefits were not
denied based on the employees’ noncompliance. Rather, the
Commission found that the certification form was a “reasonable
and unintrusive requirement,” that “has only a slight and
unintrusive impact on the teachers’ work and welfare” while
supporting the board’s interest in combating sick leave abuse.
The Commission noted that its result was limited to restraining
arbitration based on sick leave being denied for the sole reason
that employees refused to certify their absences were due to
illness or due to a funeral, stating: “We stress that our result
is predicated on the limited and undisputed facts of this case.”
Newark, 10 NJPER at 552; see also Troy v. Rutgers, 168 N.J. 354,
383 (2001) (“Questions concerning whether subjects are
mandatorily negotiable should be made on a case-by-case basis.”)
As Newark is factually distinguishable from the instant case and
constrained by its particular circumstances, we do not find it to
be persuasive precedent. By contrast, Burlington, decided much

P.E.R.C. NO. 2026-46 13.
more recently and affirmed by the Appellate Division, is nearly
identical factually to the circumstances herein.
ORDER
The request of the Mount Laurel Board of Education for a
restraint of binding arbitration of the Mount Laurel Education
Association’s grievance is denied.
BY ORDER OF THE COMMISSION
Chair Hennessy-Shotter, Commissioners Eaton, Davey, Hines, and
Papero voted in favor of this decision. None opposed.
Commissioner Higgins was not present.
ISSUED: June 25, 2026
Trenton, New Jersey
